title: 8th International Open Search Symposium – A review (day three)
content:
The third and final day of #ossym started on a controversial note. The keynote by Aline Blankertz from Structural Integrity brought in valuable new angles to the open search discussion. She argued that openness enables AI and further deepens dependencies.

Aline stated that people “like openness because it encourages sharing and transparency”.
But she also pointed out that openness feeds AI, because AI is best at exploiting openness effectively. It takes the open web and closes it by encouraging people to use a chatbot that delivers the answers easily!

One example she mentioned, which illustrates the situation, was Wikipedia.
Wikimedia and Google used to have a mutual dependence. Wikimedia needed visibility and Google needed good content! Google used to make donations. But Wikipedia page views have fallen by over a third between 2020 and 2025. Wikipedia cannot do anything because of their commitment to openness. And it seems that as Wikipedia becomes less visible, Wikipedia might decline.

Aline concluded: High quality content should not be free!

title: 8th International Open Search Symposium – A review (day two)
content:
3 days in the name of European digital sovereignty! The 8th Open Search Symposium #ossym, which was kindly supported by the German Aerospace Center, united roundabout 100 participants in Berlin and online. – continued

The morning of the second conference day was dedicated to legal and societal sessions, while the afternoon called for active participation in the form of parallel workshops.

The day kicked off with a keynote by Dr. Michael Granitzer from University of Passau, who unlocked potential scenarios of agentic information access via the OWI: “From an Open Web Index to Agentic Information Access”.
In his talk Michael shared how the future of search with AI agents could potentially look like. He predicts that the search ecosystem is changing drastically in various ways:

1. The future of search will be human-agent collaborative set-ups. Agents will become the interface between humans and information and processes; the Web will become their medium.
2. Agents will develop new knowledge by communicating between each other.
3. Small models that operate on well curated data points might be able to compete with bigger models

title: 8th International Open Search Symposium – A review (day one)
content:
On the morning of 7 October, the conference kicked off at CODE University of Applied Sciences in Berlin.
First on the mic were Peter Ruppel, President of CODE University of Applied Sciences and Fabian Geier, Professor of Philosophy at CODE University who both welcomed the participants with dedicated kick-off addresses.

“Sovereignty has become a political buzzword. This community can give it substance and it can share how it can look in practice, how to comply, how it can be governed and how it can earn trust from users.” said Peter Ruppel in his welcome address.

„It is pretty clear we are a bit cornered in Europe. In an era where bullying becomes the norm, it is unwise to not be in charge of the technology that we run our societies on.“ stated Fabian Geier.

“This is a conference for Europeans who are builders! (…) I am thankful that OSF is here and to all the people doing the work to help us become a bit more independent as Europeans and not just be on the receiving end of power but built autonomy through technology!” he added, expressing hope for hands-on solutions being shaped in Europe and underlining the importance of conferences like #ossym.

title: We were ON AIR! On Deutschlandfunk, to be more precise
content:
In addition to OpenWebSearch.eu project leader Prof. Dr. Michael Granitzer from the University of Passau, Charlotte Werther, our lawyer in the OSF-PriDI* team is also featured. She explains why the index, developed as part of OpenWebSearch.EU and studied by the PriDI project, is currently permitted for research purposes only.

It’s worth a listen! The segment is available here (in German).

*PriDI – our legal research project on “Privacy-Enhancing Digital Infrastructures” examines the legal framework for operating a European web index and develops concrete templates for developers.

title: Online Event: “Europa in der Datenfalle – Warum es mehr digitale Souveränität bei Webdaten braucht”
content:
Anyone searching the web almost always uses a non-European search engine. Anyone training AI systems needs web data – and here, too, large corporations from the U.S. and China dominate. Europe is currently heavily dependent on overseas servies within the digital sector. This is not only an economic problem but also poses a threat to European values and the democratic order.

That is why we keep asking some urgent questions:

  • Why is web data so important for the (digital) economy?
  • What opportunities does a European web data infrastructure offer – both economically and socially?
  • And what specific steps must Germany and Europe take now?

    • We provide answers in our paper commissioned by the Heinrich Böll Foundation, “Why We Need More Digital Sovereignty Over Web Data,” which will be published in German on boell.de on November 23.
    We will discuss these findings on November 24 in the following panel set-up:

  • Dr. Stefan Voigt, co-founder and board member of the Open Search Foundation e.V., co-author of the study
  • Maike Scholz, Group Compliance, Head of the “Digital Ethics” Squad, Deutsche Telekom AG

title: For something to be feasible, it must be measurable! The ZenDiS Sovereignty Check
content:
German and European policymakers want us to achieve digital sovereignty. But what does that actually mean? When are we digitally sovereign, and what conditions must be met for that to happen?

The question, then, is: How do you actually measure digital sovereignty?

The Center for Digital Sovereignty in Public Administration (ZenDiS) addressed this question in the spring of 2026. To this end, ZenDiS developed a so-called “Sovereignty Check” for public administration. This check is based on clearly defined criteria across four categories, designed to make digital sovereignty measurable: –

  • Organization and Capabilities – An organization’s management and governance capabilities
  • Digital Applications and Services – the design and interchangeability of the applications used, as well as control over these applications
  • Information and Data – data ownership and data sovereignty
  • Operations and Infrastructure – technical and organizational operational sovereignty

title: “Boosting Digital Sovereignty” – Academic Conference on Open Web Data and Europe’s Independence on the Web | Media Release
content:
Starnberg, September 29, 2026 – Web data is a key resource for AI training and independent web search. But how can Europe build an open, independent, and diverse web infrastructure? The Open Search Symposium #ossym2026 is dedicated to this central question. Experts from the fields of computer science, law, ethics, economics, and civil society will gather at CODE University of Applied Sciences in Berlin to discuss developments surrounding a European infrastructure for web search and AI. The program includes keynote speeches, academic presentations,panel discussions, and workshops. Topics to be addressed include:

  • Open Web Indexes
  • Federated search and search quality
  • Large language models, generative AI, retrieval-augmented generation
  • Georeferencing of web content, as well as geospatial search and analysis
  • Sustainability and legal, ethical, and social issues

    • related to Internet search and web data.

title: Various European Commission consultations
content:
An Open Web Data Infrastructure for Europe: We’re actively helping to shape European policy and legislation!

We completed the OpenWebSearch.EU project in April this year. Nevertheless, the OpenWebSearch Initiative, which brings together many partners from the OWS project and new stakeholders from research and industry, continues to work tirelessly on and for the Open Web Index (OWI).

The initiative not only aims to develop the infrastructure further, but is also committed to creating the framework conditions for a European Web Data Infrastructure. Shaping European policy and influencing legislation in support of an open European Web Data Infrastructure are, and will remain, key tasks of the initiative and the OSF.

We take every opportunity to emphasize the importance of a web data infrastructure for Europe!

With this mission in mind, we have, over the past few months, submitted comments on various European Commission consultations in collaboration with the OpenWebSearch Initiative and the PriDI project. In these consultations, citizens and other stakeholders can provide feedback on the Commission’s planned policy and legislative initiatives.

title: German panel discussion in partnership with the Weizenbaum Institute: register now!
content:
As part of #ossym 2026, we are delighted to invite you, in partnership with the Weizenbaum Institute, to an evening event featuring a panel discussion in Berlin. Please note that the event will be held entirely in German.

  • What: Panel discussion followed by networking (including snacks)
  • When: 8 October 2026, 7.00 pm
  • Where: Weizenbaum Institute, Hardenbergstrasse 23, 10623 Berlin

    • The development of competitive European services in the field of artificial intelligence – particularly in innovative approaches such as agent-based AI and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) – requires access to valid, large-scale web data. At present, the value generated from this publicly accessible data on the internet is almost exclusively controlled by a handful of non-European monopolists. This lack of transparency poses massive risks for Europe: distorted information, one-sidedly trained AI models and products that do not reflect European values and legislation jeopardise our digital sovereignty and democratic discourse.
